singleton.title: Shared configuration is not a global access pass
singleton.scenario: A small application reads configuration once at startup. Every feature then uses that read-only configuration.
singleton.excess: To avoid passing a parameter, put configuration, user sessions and shopping carts in a singleton that any business method can access.
singleton.cost: Dependencies become hidden and tests share state. Requests can accidentally share user data. A singleton also cannot guarantee one shared object across processes.
singleton.simpler: Create configuration at startup and pass it through constructors or the existing dependency-injection container. Keep user state scoped to each request.
singleton.reconsider: Constrain lifetime when a resource genuinely must have one instance per process and ownership of initialization, concurrent access and disposal is clear. If a container already manages that instance, a global accessor adds nothing.

factory-method.title: One email sender does not need a creation hierarchy
factory-method.scenario: Notifications use only email, and the sender is created once at application startup.
factory-method.excess: Replace a single constructor call with an abstract workflow, creation hook, email subclass and subclass registry.
factory-method.cost: Understanding one creation step requires several files and inheritance rules, without any real product to substitute.
factory-method.simpler: Construct the email sender directly. Pass it into the workflow when tests need a replacement.
factory-method.reconsider: Use Factory Method when subclasses must choose products inside a shared, stable workflow. If you only need centralized creation, a factory function is enough.

abstract-factory.title: Changing a color does not create a product family
abstract-factory.scenario: The page has one kind of button. Changing the theme only changes colors and font sizes.
abstract-factory.excess: Build a separate factory and button implementation for every color, plus interfaces for checkboxes and inputs that do not exist yet.
abstract-factory.cost: Style settings become classes. Adding a control requires changing every factory before any coordinated product family is needed.
abstract-factory.simpler: Use theme variables or configuration with one button component. Do not treat visual settings alone as product families.
abstract-factory.reconsider: Use Abstract Factory when several product types must be replaced together and each family has distinct implementations and compatibility constraints.

builder.title: Three clear options do not need ten build calls
builder.scenario: An export needs a format, filename and compression flag. The language already offers named arguments or an options object.
builder.excess: Turn every option into a build step, then add a director, builder interface and intermediate-state objects.
builder.cost: Calls become longer. You must also guard against missing required steps, repeated builds and options left over from previous use.
builder.simpler: Use named arguments or a typed options object. Validate required fields and defaults at the construction boundary.
builder.reconsider: Use Builder when assembly genuinely happens in stages, some combinations are invalid, or one assembly process must produce different representations.

prototype.title: Copying a card does not require a prototype registry
prototype.scenario: Cards contain a title and tags. They are cheap to construct, with no large set of preconfigured templates.
prototype.excess: Introduce a prototype registry, cloning interface and layered copy policies for simple data, including database connections in the clone.
prototype.cost: Shallow copies can share mutable tag lists. Deep copies can mishandle resources. Straightforward initialization becomes a question of copying semantics.
prototype.simpler: Construct cards directly or use an explicit copy function. Copy the tag collection deliberately and do not clone external resources.
prototype.reconsider: Define a cloning protocol when independent instances must come from complex preconfigured objects and the boundary between copied state and shared resources is clear.

adapter.title: If both interfaces can change, align them first
adapter.scenario: The same team owns the payment caller and new payment component. Neither interface has been published externally.
adapter.excess: Keep two easily unified pay and charge interfaces and add adapters in both directions. Treat authorization and capture as mere naming differences.
adapter.cost: Unit conversion, error mapping and tests gain another layer. Different business semantics can cause incorrect payment behavior.
adapter.simpler: Agree on amount units, operation meaning and errors. When both sides can change, implement the same contract directly.
adapter.reconsider: Adapt an unmodifiable legacy SDK or external service at the boundary when its operation genuinely matches yours. Test unit conversions and error mapping explicitly.

bridge.title: One changing dimension does not need two hierarchies
bridge.scenario: The system sends only ordinary notifications, through either email or SMS.
bridge.excess: Build separate hierarchies for message forms and delivery channels, anticipating urgent and encrypted forms that are not needed yet.
bridge.cost: Tracing one delivery crosses two abstractions, and the team maintains combination rules for nonexistent requirements.
bridge.simpler: Let the notification service depend on one delivery interface and inject an email or SMS implementation.
bridge.reconsider: Use Bridge when message forms and channels both evolve independently and inheritance combinations start multiplying. Separate two real dimensions, not imagined ones.

composite.title: A flat shopping list does not need a pretend tree
composite.scenario: The cart is a list of products. A bundle is just an indivisible product SKU.
composite.excess: Give every product a child-management interface and wrap the flat list in a tree. Make leaves implement meaningless add and remove operations.
composite.cost: Recursion and empty methods add work. Shared references or cycles can later cause duplicate pricing or endless traversal.
composite.simpler: Sum the product list directly. Use explicit pricing rules when bundles do not have uniform recursive semantics.
composite.reconsider: Use Composite when bundles can contain bundles, leaves and containers meaningfully support the same operation, and the structure really is a tree.

decorator.title: A fixed coffee recipe does not need five wrappers
decorator.scenario: The menu has two fixed recipes. Ingredients cannot be freely combined or changed at runtime.
decorator.excess: Split each recipe into layers of decorators and let wrapper order secretly determine discounts, pricing and ingredient conflicts.
decorator.cost: The final price is hard to trace. Ordering becomes an implicit business rule, and testing each layer does not establish that a combination is correct.
decorator.simpler: Use recipe data and one pricing function. Express incompatible ingredients and discount order as explicit rules.
decorator.reconsider: Use Decorator when added responsibilities compose independently behind the same interface and ordering semantics are clear. Do not use wrappers to hide tightly coupled rules.

facade.title: A short startup function does not need a general manager
facade.scenario: The application has one entry point. A short function already expresses database and logging startup clearly.
facade.excess: Add a facade class, then funnel unrelated payment, user and reporting features into the same entry point.
facade.cost: The facade becomes a giant object. Changes affect unrelated callers and hide failures that callers need to handle.
facade.simpler: Keep the explicit startup function. Let each business module provide its own focused interface.
facade.reconsider: Offer a focused facade when several callers repeatedly orchestrate the same complex subsystem and common tasks have stable boundaries. Retain necessary low-level access.

flyweight.title: Ten trees do not justify a shared object pool
flyweight.scenario: The map contains few trees. Species and color data are small, with no measured memory pressure.
flyweight.excess: Build a flyweight cache, key generator and eviction mechanism in advance. Put individual positions and mutable colors into shared objects too.
flyweight.cost: The cache consumes memory itself. Sharing mutable state can make a change to one tree affect other trees.
flyweight.simpler: Start with ordinary objects and measure memory. If sharing becomes necessary, share only immutable species data and keep positions per instance.
flyweight.reconsider: Separate intrinsic and extrinsic state when many objects duplicate expensive immutable data and measurements show meaningful savings. Define the cache lifetime as well.

proxy.title: Cheap access does not need another interception layer
proxy.scenario: The preview displays one small image. The existing image component already handles lazy loading and caching.
proxy.excess: Write another image proxy to duplicate caching and lazy loading, and quietly swallow loading errors.
proxy.cost: Cache invalidation and recovery get a second implementation. Callers may believe access succeeded while receiving stale data or no result.
proxy.simpler: Use the existing component's loading facilities and expose loading and failure states. Call cheap operations directly.
proxy.reconsider: Add a proxy when costly resources, permissions or remote access need control behind the original interface. Timeouts, failures and consistency still need explicit handling.

chain-of-responsibility.title: Two stable amount ranges do not need a ticket pipeline
chain-of-responsibility.scenario: Support tickets go to an agent or supervisor based on two fixed, mutually exclusive amount ranges.
chain-of-responsibility.excess: Turn two conditions into a dynamically assembled chain without defining termination, unhandled requests or ordering effects.
chain-of-responsibility.cost: Routing becomes opaque. Changing order can change the assignee, and missing a fallback can silently lose a ticket.
chain-of-responsibility.simpler: Use one explicit routing function that returns the assignee. Test amount boundaries and the fallback path.
chain-of-responsibility.reconsider: Use a chain when independent handlers must be added, removed or reordered and requests can try them sequentially. Define termination and unhandled outcomes.

command.title: One immediate button action does not need a command bus
command.scenario: A toolbar button clears temporary filters. There is no undo, queueing, replay or recording requirement.
command.excess: Create a command class, executor, registry and history for one call, claiming every side effect can automatically be undone.
command.cost: A simple event crosses several dispatch layers. Undoing an external email or payment is not just running a method backward.
command.simpler: Call the clear function from the event handler. Design business compensation separately when external side effects need correction.
command.reconsider: Make requests into commands when they need independent storage, delayed execution, composition or controlled undo. Define arguments, results and undo boundaries.

interpreter.title: One age check does not need a rule language
interpreter.scenario: The rule is fixed: age at least 18 and membership active. Only developers change it.
interpreter.excess: Invent expression syntax, a parser and interpreter nodes for two conditions, then handwrite precedence and type conversions as it grows.
interpreter.cost: You maintain syntax errors, safety limits and performance as well as the rule. Complex input makes parsing and execution harder to control.
interpreter.simpler: Compose explicit predicate functions. For a genuinely complex rule language, prefer a mature parser or rule engine.
interpreter.reconsider: Evaluate Interpreter when a small, stable grammar represents expressions assembled from data and evaluated repeatedly. Do not grow a teaching grammar into a homemade general-purpose language.

iterator.title: An array already knows how to iterate
iterator.scenario: The playlist is an in-memory array. All you need is to read every song in order.
iterator.excess: Rewrite hasNext, next and cursor management for the built-in array, forbidding callers from using the language's standard iteration syntax.
iterator.cost: Boundaries, termination and mutation behavior need duplicate maintenance, with an interface inconsistent with built-in collections.
iterator.simpler: Use built-in iterators, loops or generators and follow the existing collection protocol.
iterator.reconsider: Implement the standard iteration protocol when paging, lazy loading or a special structure must hide storage details. Do not invent another traversal API.

mediator.title: One search data flow does not need an all-purpose coordinator
mediator.scenario: The search field sends a query to its page, which displays matching results. Data flows in one direction.
mediator.excess: Register every control with a global mediator and put requests, rendering, caching and authorization in the coordinator.
mediator.cost: Controls lose dependencies, but the central object becomes a new coupling hub. Local changes require understanding hidden page-wide scheduling.
mediator.simpler: Express one-way data flow with page state and callbacks. Keep responsibilities in their own modules.
mediator.reconsider: Extract bounded coordination when peer components genuinely form a web of bidirectional dependencies. Keep it from becoming a global manager.

memento.title: An editor without undo does not need snapshot history
memento.scenario: The editor saves only the final content. There is no requirement to undo or restore earlier states.
memento.excess: Deep-copy the whole document on every keystroke, including connections, caches and large attachments, into an unlimited history.
memento.cost: Frequent input increases memory and copying costs. Snapshots can retain sensitive state or resources that cannot be copied safely.
memento.simpler: Keep only current content. When recovery is needed, first define recoverable state, history capacity and snapshot frequency.
memento.reconsider: Use Memento to restore internal state without exposing its implementation. For large documents, evaluate incremental logs, persistent structures or specialized storage first.

observer.title: One stock refresh does not need a global event bus
observer.scenario: A stock change updates one display on the current page. There are no other independent subscribers.
observer.excess: Connect all modules through string events on a global bus, treating in-process notifications as reliable message delivery.
observer.cost: Sources, ordering and subscription cleanup are hard to trace. Stale subscriptions cause duplicate updates, and process exits lose unpersisted notifications.
observer.simpler: Refresh the display through a callback or shared page state. Use mature messaging infrastructure for cross-process delivery, retries and persistence.
observer.reconsider: Use Observer when one publisher genuinely needs multiple independent, dynamically subscribed receivers. Specify unsubscribe, exception and reentrancy behavior.

state.title: Play and stop do not need a collection of state classes
state.scenario: The player has only playing and stopped states, few events and clear, stable transition rules.
state.excess: Create a class per state plus context and transition objects, scattering transition rules across files.
state.cost: Tracing one click crosses multiple objects. Legal transitions are no longer visible together, and cyclic calls become easier to introduce.
state.simpler: Use an enum and a clear switch to express states and transitions. Test invalid events centrally.
state.reconsider: Use state objects when behavior differs substantially by state and conditions spread across methods. Prefer a mature state-machine library for complex workflows.

strategy.title: One stable payment method does not need a strategy family
strategy.scenario: Checkout only accepts cards. No other channel or runtime switching is needed in the near term.
strategy.excess: Anticipate future channels with a payment strategy interface, factory, registry and several empty implementations.
strategy.cost: A single payment needs selection and assembly. The interface starts answering requirements that do not exist yet.
strategy.simpler: Call the card payment function directly. For one or two stable approaches, a clear conditional can also be enough.
strategy.reconsider: Extract strategies when real wallet or points rules evolve independently and follow the same task contract. Do not force refunds and authorization into one interface just because they concern payment.

template-method.title: Do not lock an unstable workflow into a base class
template-method.scenario: CSV and JSON imports are still experimental. Validation, saving and error recovery often happen in different orders.
template-method.excess: Force both to inherit one importer because method names look similar, then add hooks and switches to bypass the fixed workflow.
template-method.cost: Subclasses inherit ordering constraints. Changing the base affects every implementation, and multiplying hooks suggests the common skeleton may not exist.
template-method.simpler: Extract genuinely shared small functions and compose each workflow explicitly. Do not fix an inheritance template prematurely.
template-method.reconsider: Use Template Method when the read-transform-save skeleton is stable and subclasses replace only a few steps. Use strategies or composition for freely recombined runtime behavior.

visitor.title: Growing node types make every visitor more expensive
visitor.scenario: The file tree only needs size calculation, but node types keep growing: links, archives and remote files.
visitor.excess: Build a visitor protocol for one operation and require every visitor to gain another method whenever a node type is added.
visitor.cost: Adding an element becomes a cross-file change. Visitors may also demand internal data that breaks node encapsulation.
visitor.simpler: Keep size calculation on nodes or use language-supported pattern matching. Do not expose all internal representation for visitors.
visitor.reconsider: Use Visitor when node types are stable but external operations such as statistics and export keep growing. Accept the maintenance cost of introducing a new node type.
